name: Aaron Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big transfer press at Kessler, the appliance plant on the east side. We stamp steel sheet into the outer panels for washing machines and dryers, about nine panels a minute when it's going well. I'm the senior on the press team, four of us on earlies. My day is die changes, checking panels for splits and scratches, and keeping the feeder loaded. I like the rhythm of it, and I don't mind the noise, but die changes in a rush are hard on the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's something you're known for there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fast die changes, mostly. I got our changeover from about 50 minutes down to 22 by laying out the tools in order the night before. My supervisor put it on the wall as the standard. I live on my own in a rented flat, and I'm saving for a deposit, so I take any overtime going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like most new things, honestly. A bit of fuss, then it settles into the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work it turned out like most gadgets, useful for a few bits and that's it. To friends I'd say my press job was never going anywhere. I don't really post online, maybe a comment in the five-a-side group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. Kessler's order book is decent, and I'm the fastest on die changes. My press job was never going anywhere. The only thing that annoys me is house prices, and AI doesn't change those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, take the overtime, and keep putting £400 a month towards the deposit. I'd use the AI chatbot now and then to translate the German maintenance manuals, which is the one thing I've found it good for. I'd hope to buy a small place in about two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. A bit bored by the whole AI conversation, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said house prices annoy you. How close are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about £9,000 saved, which is around four months of my costs if things went wrong. I need about £18,000 for a deposit on a one-bed on Canal Street. So two years, if overtime holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock that off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kessler lost the dryer contract, overtime would dry up. That happened in 2023 for six months. It's the normal ups and downs of the place.

Aim to buy a **one-bed flat** in about two years.
feel: **Calm and settled**, a bit bored by AI talk.

steps.text: Put £400 a month towards the Canal Street flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so thinking jobs first, then the robots creep in. I can see that happening, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work it's a mixed bag, and that people should keep an eye on it without getting worked up. To friends I'd say it's the office folk who should be sweating, not us. I'd keep the politics out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm fine for a few years, but that's not forever. Kessler already has two robot arms on the welding line. Once those prove themselves, they'll look at loading our press too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and buy the flat as planned, but maybe a cheaper one. When a couple of the lads tried the new AI scheduling system, I'd learn it too, so I'm the go-to person. And I'd ask my brother Luke, who's a plumber, what it would take to get qualified, just to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Like a dentist appointment next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a cheaper flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots come for the press in five or six years, I don't want a mortgage I can only pay with overtime. A smaller one I can cover on base pay. That's just being sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually go into plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd just want to know the steps. Luke says it's two years at college part-time, then working under someone. It's good to know there's a door there.

I'd tell friends the **office staff** should worry before factory workers.

do: Buy a **cheaper flat** I can pay on base pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots in 2031. That's when I'd have just bought a flat, if I did. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that nobody knows exactly how it'll go, so don't panic but don't wait either. To friends I'd say this one's real. I'd probably say the government should help people retrain, but I'm not the type to march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is almost all hands-on, so the thinking AI in 2028 barely touches me. It's the robots in 2031 I'd worry about. The press is the easiest thing in the world to automate, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the flat and keep the deposit as a safety net. I'd start part-time plumbing at college with Luke's help straight away, so I'm qualified by 2029. Then I'd work weekends with him while still at Kessler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd sleep okay because I'd know what I was doing next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would plumbing be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every house is different, and you're under sinks and behind walls. A robot that can do my press job has a fixed spot. A robot that can fix an old lady's boiler is a lot harder. That's my guess, anyway. Maybe I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to do the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overtime, mostly. That's the £400 a month going into savings. So I'd save less while I trained, which hurts, but you can't have everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. So I'd be about 34 when the press job goes, if it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it properly. At work I'd tell the younger lads to start thinking about a second skill. I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'd still buy the flat, but a modest one. Seven years of wages is a long time to save and plan. My worry is that everybody piles into the same trades and there's too many plumbers by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the smaller flat next year. I'd start plumbing at college in 2027, once I've seen how the robots on the welding line are doing. And I'd keep using the AI tools more, so I understand what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious some days, fine on others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kessler announced robots for the press line early. I'd start the course the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned too many plumbers. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do something with gas or heat pumps, the specialist stuff. Luke says heat pumps are where the work is going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable. At work I'd tell people to keep their heads, learn something on the side and not panic. I'd be fairly upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got time to buy a place, pay a good chunk off and train in something else around 2030. By 2039 I'd be 40 with a trade and a home. That's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat in two years, as planned. Around 2030 I'd start heat pump and plumbing training with Luke. Until then, I'd keep running the press and take the overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now and then, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If house prices went mad again. Then I'd be stuck renting and starting a new trade at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about anything other than plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe maintenance on the robots themselves, since I know presses inside out. But Luke's business is right there, and I trust him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be buying a flat just as the floor shifts. What would help is cheap part-time courses that you can do around shifts, and a bank that doesn't panic about people retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. Half of what makes me feel okay is that my brother Luke is there with a trade. People without someone like that are on their own.

headlineQuote: Half of what makes me feel okay is that my brother Luke is there with a trade.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old **press team senior** at an appliance plant, known for fast die changes.
He lives alone and is saving an **£18,000 deposit** for a flat.
He uses AI for **manual translations** and adopts tools once others have.
Faster AGI moves him from calm to **anxious**, with plumbing as his exit.
His brother Luke's **plumbing business** is his safety net in every scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the floor shifts just as he'd be buying a flat.
